chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Constraints are rules the database enforces on its own
A constraint is a rule attached to a table or column that the database checks on every insert, update and delete, no matter which application, script or person made the change. That is why they matter so much for testing. UI validation can be bypassed by calling the API, API validation can be bypassed by a bulk import or a hand-written UPDATE, but a constraint can't be bypassed at all (unless someone disables it, 4.3). So you test data rules at three layers: the UI (friendly message), the API (correct status code and error body), and the database (the last line of defence). The tester's question for every rule is "which layers enforce it?" A rule enforced in the UI only is a defect waiting for the first API client or import.
## Primary keys: one identity per row
A primary key (PK) uniquely identifies each row. It must be unique and can't be NULL, and each table has at most one (though it can span several columns). attendance and leave_balances show the two common designs:
-- Surrogate key: a meaningless auto-generated number
attendance_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY

-- Composite (natural) key: the combination is the identity
PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, leave_type_id)          -- leave_balances: one balance per employee per leave type

Test the rule directly, inside a rolled-back transaction (0.4):
```sql
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO leave_balances (employee_id, leave_type_id, balance) VALUES (1, 1, 5.0);
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1-1' for key 'leave_balances.PRIMARY'
INSERT INTO leave_balances (employee_id, leave_type_id, balance) VALUES (NULL, 1, 5.0);
-- ERROR 1048 (23000): Column 'employee_id' cannot be null
ROLLBACK;
```

## Things worth knowing about keys:
Gaps are normal. Auto-increment numbers are consumed even when the insert fails or is rolled back, so IDs 5, 6, 8 don't mean row 7 was deleted. Never write a test that expects consecutive IDs.
Keys can run out. A signed INT ends at 2,147,483,647, and inserts then fail with a duplicate key error on a busy table. Check the headroom:

| SELECT table_name, auto_increment | FROM   information_schema.tables |
|---|---|
| WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND auto_increment IS NOT NULL | ORDER  BY auto_increment DESC; |

An auto_increment value approaching 2 billion in a real environment deserves a report. (MySQL 8 keeps the counter in the table metadata, so it survives restarts, while 5.7 could reset it to MAX(id)+1, which can reissue the IDs of deleted rows.)
Never put business meaning in a surrogate key. If a screen shows the ID as an "employee number", customers will care about gaps and the order.
UUID keys (CHAR(36), BINARY(16) or a native UUID) avoid guessable IDs and conflicts across systems. They take more space and, when random, make inserts slower. Test that the API rejects malformed IDs cleanly.
## Foreign keys: the recap, plus the delete rule
Chapter 4.3 covered foreign keys in depth (missing FKs, disabled checks, orphans, referential actions). Two additional facts. First, the actions are visible in the catalog:
```sql
SELECT constraint_name, table_name, referenced_table_name, update_rule, delete_rule
FROM   information_schema.referential_constraints
WHERE  constraint_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name IN ('leave_requests','appointments')
ORDER  BY table_name, constraint_name;
```

constraint_name        | table_name     | referenced_table_name | update_rule | delete_rule
## appointments_ibfk_1    | appointments   | customers             | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION
## appointments_ibfk_2    | appointments   | services              | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION
## appointments_ibfk_3    | appointments   | employees             | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION
## leave_requests_ibfk_1  | leave_requests | employees             | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION
## leave_requests_ibfk_2  | leave_requests | leave_types           | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION
## leave_requests_ibfk_3  | leave_requests | employees             | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION

NO ACTION (some versions display RESTRICT) means "block the delete or update if children exist", so every relationship here blocks deletes. A CASCADE in this column is a red flag worth reading twice: ON DELETE CASCADE from customers to appointments means that deleting a customer silently deletes their appointment history. That might be intended, but a tester should check that a UI "delete customer" doesn't wipe records the business needs for audit or billing. Second, when a FK exists, the child column needs an index for joins and parent deletes to be fast. MySQL InnoDB creates one automatically, while PostgreSQL and SQL Server don't (8.5).
## Unique constraints: duplicates the database refuses
A UNIQUE constraint says no two rows may share the same value (or the same combination of values). Unlike a PK, unique columns may be nullable. Points to test:
-- Case: with a case-insensitive collation, these clash (2.5)
```sql
INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, hire_date) VALUES ('X', 'Y', 'ASHA@example.com', '2026-01-01');
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'ASHA@example.com' for key 'employees.email'
```

-- Composite: the pair must be unique, not each column
```sql
INSERT INTO attendance (employee_id, work_date) VALUES (1, '2026-09-14');
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1-2026-09-14' for key 'attendance.employee_id'
```

Notice the second key name is employee_id. When a unique constraint is declared without a name, MySQL names it after its first column, so error messages and index listings can be confusing. Ask for named constraints (uq_attendance_emp_date). Also remember what the message leaks: a raw "Duplicate entry 'ASHA@example.com'" shown to a user reveals that the email exists (an account-enumeration risk) and exposes internal names.
NULLs in unique columns behave differently per database
```sql
INSERT INTO ux_demo (code) VALUES (NULL), (NULL);     -- MySQL and PostgreSQL: succeeds (NULL never equals NULL)
                                                      -- SQL Server: the second NULL is rejected
INSERT INTO ux_demo (code) VALUES ('A1');
INSERT INTO ux_demo (code) VALUES ('a1');
-- MySQL (case-insensitive collation): ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'a1' for key 'ux_demo.uq_code'
-- PostgreSQL (case-sensitive): succeeds, so 'A1' and 'a1' coexist
```

Two consequences. An "optional but unique" field (a national ID, a phone number) can legitimately be blank for many rows in MySQL and PostgreSQL, so don't call multiple blank rows duplicates. And the same schema behaves differently across databases (6.5). Also test "blank" carefully: the UI may save an empty field as '' rather than NULL, and '' is a real value, so the second blank submission fails with a duplicate error. That is a classic defect ("I can't leave phone empty twice") caused by not converting blanks to NULL.
## NOT NULL, DEFAULT and CHECK
NOT NULL forbids missing values, and a DEFAULT supplies a value when the insert leaves the column out. Both are direct sources of test cases (8.2). CHECK enforces an arbitrary condition on a row, and we added one to leave_requests:
-- Pre-check before adding any constraint: does existing data already violate it? (6.4)
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, days FROM leave_requests WHERE NOT (days > 0 AND days <= 365);   -- 0 rows, safe to add
```

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days)
VALUES (1, 1, '2026-12-01', '2026-12-01', 0);
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_leave_days' is violated.
ROLLBACK;
```

Four CHECK gotchas: it passes when the expression is NULL (unknown counts as not violated), so a nullable column needs NOT NULL as well; MySQL before 8.0.16 and some old tools accept the syntax and silently ignore it, so verify with a real violating insert instead of trusting the DDL; a CHECK can only see the same row (no lookups to other tables, which is what triggers are for, 8.3); and MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQL Server enforce it in all supported versions.
## Indexes: how the database finds rows fast
An index is a separate, sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database jump to matching rows without reading the entire table, like the index at the back of a book. The trade-offs are that reads get faster, writes get slower (every insert or update must maintain each index), and storage grows. Key facts for testers:
Primary keys and unique constraints are implemented by unique indexes. The "duplicate" error above is the index refusing a second entry.
A composite index follows the "leftmost prefix" rule. An index on (employee_id, work_date) accelerates filters on employee_id alone, or on employee_id and work_date together, but not (efficiently) on work_date alone. Column order in an index matters.
Selectivity matters. An index on a column with few distinct values (is_deleted, status) helps little, because each value still matches a large fraction of the table.
An index only helps if the query is written to use it (sargability, 2.1): no function wrapped around the column (YEAR(work_date) = 2025), no leading wildcard (LIKE '%avi', 2.5), and no type mismatch (comparing a text column to a number forces per-row conversion, 1.2).
A covering index contains every column a query needs, so the table itself isn't touched (MySQL shows Using index).
See what indexes exist:
```sql
SHOW INDEX FROM leave_requests;
```

## Table          | Non_unique | Key_name              | Seq_in_index | Column_name
## leave_requests | 0          | PRIMARY               | 1            | leave_request_id
## leave_requests | 1          | employee_id           | 1            | employee_id
## leave_requests | 1          | leave_type_id         | 1            | leave_type_id
## leave_requests | 1          | approved_by           | 1            | approved_by

(Condensed. The real output has more columns, including Cardinality.) Non_unique = 0 marks a unique index. The three non-unique rows are the automatic indexes MySQL built for the foreign keys. Equivalents: \d leave_requests in psql, sp_helpindex 'leave_requests' in SQL Server, or the catalog views listed in 6.5.
Indexes are testable in three ways. Existence: schema drift often means QA has an index that production lacks (6.5), so performance tests that pass in QA prove nothing. Effect: does a query really use the index, and does it get faster (EXPLAIN, 8.5)? Cost: a bulk import into a heavily indexed table is much slower, and a report that was fast at 1,000 rows may crawl at a million.
Listing every constraint on a table
```sql
SELECT tc.table_name, tc.constraint_type, tc.constraint_name,
       GROUP_CONCAT(kcu.column_name ORDER BY kcu.ordinal_position) AS columns_involved
FROM   information_schema.table_constraints tc
LEFT JOIN information_schema.key_column_usage kcu
```
| ON  kcu.constraint_schema = tc.constraint_schema | AND kcu.table_name        = tc.table_name | AND kcu.constraint_name   = tc.constraint_name |
|---|---|---|
| WHERE  tc.table_schema = DATABASE() AND tc.table_name IN ('leave_balances','leave_requests') | GROUP  BY tc.table_name, tc.constraint_type, tc.constraint_name | ORDER  BY tc.table_name, tc.constraint_type, tc.constraint_name; |

| table_name     \| constraint_type \| constraint_name       \| columns_involved | leave_balances \| FOREIGN KEY     \| leave_balances_ibfk_1 \| employee_id | leave_balances \| FOREIGN KEY     \| leave_balances_ibfk_2 \| leave_type_id |
|---|---|---|
| leave_balances \| PRIMARY KEY     \| PRIMARY               \| employee_id,leave_type_id | leave_requests \| CHECK           \| chk_leave_days        \| NULL | leave_requests \| FOREIGN KEY     \| leave_requests_ibfk_1 \| employee_id |
| leave_requests \| FOREIGN KEY     \| leave_requests_ibfk_2 \| leave_type_id | leave_requests \| FOREIGN KEY     \| leave_requests_ibfk_3 \| approved_by | leave_requests \| PRIMARY KEY     \| PRIMARY               \| leave_request_id |

CHECK rows have no columns here because key_column_usage only covers keys. To read the actual expression, query information_schema.check_constraints (check_clause). Notice what the list does not contain: there is no unique constraint on leave_requests (so identical requests can be submitted twice) and none on payroll (6.3). Absence is a finding.
## Testing a constraint end to end
For each business rule that a constraint should protect, write one test that tries to break it at every layer and asserts the same outcome: rejected, a clean user-facing message, and no data change.
```ts
test('duplicate employee email is rejected in UI, API and DB', async ({ page, request }) => {
  const email = `qa_${Date.now()}_dup@example.com`;
  const payload = { firstName: 'QA_Dup', lastName: 'Tester', email, departmentId: 2, hireDate: '2025-01-01' };
```

```ts
  const first = await request.post('/api/employees', { data: payload });
  expect(first.status()).toBe(201);
```

```ts
  const second = await request.post('/api/employees', { data: payload });      // API layer
  expect(second.status()).toBe(409);                                           // a clean conflict, not a 500
  expect(await second.text()).not.toMatch(/SQLSTATE|Duplicate entry|constraint|employees\.email/i);   // no DB internals leaked
```

  await page.goto('/employees/new');                                           // UI layer
  await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('QA_Dup');
  await page.getByLabel('Last name').fill('Tester');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email.toUpperCase());                    // case variant, since the DB collation is case-insensitive
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/already exists|already registered/i)).toBeVisible();

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees WHERE email = ?', [email]);   // DB layer
  expect(rows[0].n).toBe(1);                                                   // exactly one row survived
  // cleanup in a finally block (7.2)
});
```

A compact matrix for planning:

| Constraint | Negative test | Expected outcome at every layer | PK | Duplicate or NULL key (DB-level only, app rarely exposes it) | DB error; app never produces it |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FK | Child with a missing parent; delete a parent with children | Rejected with a friendly message; no orphan | UNIQUE | Exact, case-variant and whitespace-variant duplicates; two blanks | Conflict message; blanks stored as NULL where optional |
| NOT NULL | Omit the field; send null, "" and spaces | Required-field error, and "" isn't stored as a valid value | CHECK | Values just outside the rule (0, negative, 366) | Range error with the rule in plain words |
| Length/type | Max, max+1, wrong type | Validation error, and no silent truncation | Index | Existence in every environment | Same indexes everywhere (6.5) |

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The schema is an executable specification
A requirements document says what the product should do, and the schema records what the developers actually built to store it. Every column, type, nullability flag, default, enum value and constraint is a rule that someone decided on, and each one implies test cases. Testers who read the schema find bugs that testers who only click through the UI don't, because they know the boundaries the UI is hiding. Reading one table's DDL before testing its screen takes ten minutes and routinely produces dozens of scenarios.

| Turn each schema element into test ideas | In the DDL | Test ideas it implies |
|---|---|---|
| NOT NULL, no default | Omit the field, send null, send "", send spaces; each should be rejected | Nullable column |
| Blank vs NULL paths (2.3); does the screen, export and report show blanks the same way? | VARCHAR(50) | 49, 50, 51 characters; multi-byte text (a Devanagari name counts characters, not bytes; 2.4); leading and trailing spaces |
| DECIMAL(4,1) | 999.9 (max), 1000.0 (overflow), 0.05 (rounding), 2 or more decimals, negative, zero | INT |
| 0, -1, max, max+1, decimal input, text input | DATE / TIMESTAMP | Today, past, far future, leap day, 2026-02-30, time zone edges (1.2) |
| ENUM(...) | Every listed value; an unlisted value via the API; wrong case | DEFAULT 'pending' |
| Omit the field via the API and confirm the stored value | UNIQUE | Exact, case and whitespace duplicates; two blanks |
| FOREIGN KEY | Missing parent; delete or deactivate the parent; parent from a different tenant | CHECK |
| Both sides of every boundary | Composite key | Same first column with a different second, and the reverse |
| is_deleted / deleted_at | Does every screen, report and count hide deleted rows? (8.4) | created_at / updated_at |
| Set on create; changed on update; unchanged by unrelated updates | Missing constraint | "Nothing stops duplicates here, so can the UI create one?" |

## Generate the checklist from the catalog
A query can produce the first draft of test ideas for any table. This MySQL version reads information_schema.columns (a run on leave_requests, showing only the interesting columns):
```sql
SELECT column_name, column_type,
       CONCAT_WS('; ',
         CASE WHEN column_key = 'PRI' THEN 'primary key: duplicate/NULL at DB level, gaps are normal' END,
         CASE WHEN is_nullable = 'NO' AND column_default IS NULL AND extra NOT LIKE '%auto_increment%'
              THEN 'required: omit/null/blank/spaces -> rejected' END,
         CASE WHEN is_nullable = 'YES' THEN 'optional: blank vs NULL handled the same?' END,
         CASE WHEN data_type IN ('varchar','char')
              THEN CONCAT('length ', character_maximum_length, ': try ', character_maximum_length, ' and ', character_maximum_length + 1) END,
         CASE WHEN data_type = 'enum' THEN CONCAT('each value: ', column_type, '; plus one invalid') END,
         CASE WHEN data_type = 'decimal' THEN CONCAT('precision ', numeric_precision, ',', numeric_scale, ': max, max+1, extra decimals') END,
         CASE WHEN data_type IN ('date','datetime','timestamp') THEN 'past, today, future, leap day, invalid date' END,
         CASE WHEN column_default IS NOT NULL THEN CONCAT('default ', column_default, ': omit and check stored value') END,
         CASE WHEN column_key = 'UNI' THEN 'unique: duplicate, case and space variants' END,
         CASE WHEN column_key = 'MUL' THEN 'indexed/FK: missing-parent test' END
```
| ) AS test_ideas | FROM   information_schema.columns |
|---|---|
| WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'leave_requests' | ORDER  BY ordinal_position; |

## column_name      | column_type                                          | test_ideas
leave_request_id | int                                                  | primary key: duplicate/NULL at DB level, gaps are normal
employee_id      | int                                                  | required: omit/null/blank/spaces -> rejected; indexed/FK: missing-parent test
leave_type_id    | int                                                  | required: ...; indexed/FK: missing-parent test
start_date       | date                                                 | required: ...; past, today, future, leap day, invalid date
end_date         | date                                                 | required: ...; past, today, future, leap day, invalid date
days             | decimal(4,1)                                         | required: ...; precision 4,1: max, max+1, extra decimals
status           | enum('pending','approved','rejected','cancelled')    | default pending: omit and check stored value; each value: ...; plus one invalid
approved_by      | int                                                  | optional: blank vs NULL handled the same?; indexed/FK: missing-parent test
created_at       | timestamp                                            | optional: ...; past, today, future, leap day, invalid date; default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP: omit and check stored value

It is a starting point, not a finished test design. The value is in what a human sees in it. For example, days is a free number alongside two dates, so the schema doesn't tie them together (the CHECK only bounds days), which suggests testing whether the app lets days = 6 for a one-day range. And approved_by is nullable, with no rule linking it to status, so nothing stops an approved request with no approver. Both are cross-column rules the database doesn't enforce (they came up as violation queries in 1.4 and 2.3), so the application must, and you should try to break them.
## Find the gaps between the layers
The most productive bug hunting is at the seams between UI, API and database rules:

| Situation | How to test | Typical defect |
|---|---|---|
| UI maxlength differs from column length | Compare getAttribute('maxlength') with the DB length (1.2) | UI allows 100, DB holds 50: error or silent truncation |
| UI dropdown lists 3 statuses, DB enum has 4 | Compare option texts with the enum values | A valid state is unreachable, or an old value is still offered |
| UI hides a field the API accepts | Send the field directly to the API | Mass assignment: a user sets status='approved' or approved_by on their own request |
| UI enforces required, API doesn't | POST without the field | A row with NULL or an empty string, breaking screens later |
| DB has a UNIQUE, UI shows a generic error | Submit a duplicate | Raw error text, a 500, or a leaked internal name |
| No DB constraint, UI blocks it | Repeat the action via API or double-click | A duplicate slips through |

```ts
test('UI limits match the database column definitions', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/employees/new');
```

```ts
  const [cols]: any = await db.execute(
    `SELECT column_name, character_maximum_length AS len FROM information_schema.columns
     WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'employees' AND column_name IN ('first_name','email')`);
```

| const uiMax: Record<string, string \| null> = { | first_name: await page.getByLabel('First name').getAttribute('maxlength'), | email:      await page.getByLabel('Email').getAttribute('maxlength'), | }; |
|---|---|---|---|
| for (const c of cols) { | expect(Number(uiMax[c.column_name]), `${c.column_name}: UI limit vs DB length ${c.len}`).toBeLessThanOrEqual(c.len); | } | }); |

A test like this catches the day someone widens a form field without a migration, or narrows a column without updating the form.
```sql
Use the schema to design data, not just checks
```
Constraints tell you the equivalence classes for test data. For days DECIMAL(4,1) with CHECK (days > 0 AND days <= 365) the classes are: valid interior (2.5), lower boundary (0.1), below the boundary (0, invalid), upper boundary (365), above (365.1, invalid), precision violation (2.55), non-numeric. Each is a row in a data-driven test. For status plus approved_by, the combinations that matter are pending-with-no-approver (valid), approved-with-approver (valid), and the suspicious pair approved-with-no-approver. Then the schema tells you what to clean up (children first, 7.2) and what to verify afterwards (which tables a "create employee" action should write, and what side effects like a balance row or a history row should exist).
## Questions to bring to developers and analysts
## Reading the schema always produces questions, and asking them early saves defects later:
"payroll has no unique constraint on employee and month. Is a second row for the same month ever valid?"
"approved_by is nullable: can an approved request have no approver, for example after an import?"
## "status is an enum: what are the allowed transitions, and who can make each one?"
"days is stored, not computed: which calendar and holiday rules produce it, and who recomputes it if the dates change?"
"Deletes are soft: which screens and jobs should ignore deleted rows?"
## "Why is email unique but phone not?"
A defect report that cites the schema is also harder to dismiss: "the leave_requests table has no rule preventing overlapping requests for one employee, and the API accepted two overlapping requests (IDs ...)".

chapters.title: 8.3 Views, Triggers & Stored Procedures

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Logic that lives inside the database
Most business logic lives in the application, but many systems keep some inside the database itself, in three kinds of objects. Views are saved queries that behave like tables. Triggers run automatically when rows change. Stored procedures (and functions) are named blocks of code you call. They matter for testers because they change data or shape it without any application code involved, so a UI test can pass or fail because of something that appears in no repository the front-end and API developers work in. Find what exists in your schema early (8.6).
## Views: a saved query with a table's clothes on
A view stores a SELECT, not data (except materialised views, below). Querying the view runs the underlying query at that moment. We created v_leave_summary:
```sql
SELECT * FROM v_leave_summary ORDER BY employee_id;
```

employee_id | employee_name | department | total_requests | approved_days | pending_requests
| 1           \| Asha Karki    \| QA         \| 3              \| 4.0           \| 1 | 2           \| Ravi Shrestha \| QA         \| 4              \| 3.0           \| 1 |
|---|---|
| 3           \| Mina Thapa    \| Finance    \| 2              \| 2.0           \| 1 | 4           \| Sita Gurung   \| HR         \| 0              \| 0.0           \| 0 |

Bikash is missing because the view filters is_deleted = 0, which is a business rule encoded in the view that every consumer inherits. Read the definition, don't guess:
```sql
SHOW CREATE VIEW v_leave_summary\G                       -- MySQL
SELECT view_definition, is_updatable, security_type FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();
-- PostgreSQL: SELECT pg_get_viewdef('v_leave_summary'::regclass, true);   SQL Server: sp_helptext 'v_leave_summary'
```

## How to test a view:
Cross-check it with an independent query (the two-formulation technique, 5.3). Write the numbers from the base tables yourself and compare:
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leave_requests lr WHERE lr.employee_id = e.employee_id)                                 AS total_requests,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(lr.days),0) FROM leave_requests lr WHERE lr.employee_id = e.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved') AS approved_days
FROM   employees e WHERE e.is_deleted = 0
```
EXCEPT
```sql
SELECT employee_id, total_requests, approved_days FROM v_leave_summary;        -- MySQL 8.0.31+; expect 0 rows (run the reverse direction too)
```

Watch for fan-out and inner-join loss inside the view (4.1). The view above left-joins both tables, so employees with no requests still appear. An inner join there would drop them silently from the dashboard that reads the view.
Views break on schema changes. Renaming or dropping a column that a view uses leaves the view invalid, and it fails only when someone queries it, often long after the migration. After every migration (6.4), run SELECT 1 FROM each_view LIMIT 1 for all views, or check information_schema.views for entries that fail.
Updatable views (simple single-table views) accept INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and pass them to the base table. WITH CHECK OPTION stops an update through the view from producing a row the view would no longer show. Test that rule if the app writes through a view.
Security views: views are a common way to expose masked or limited columns to a role (7.6). In MySQL and SQL Server a view usually runs with its definer's rights, so a tester who can query the view may see rows they couldn't read from the base table. That's often the intent, and it is worth verifying that the role's access is limited to the view and doesn't extend to the table.
Materialised views (PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server "indexed views") store the result and go stale until refreshed. A report reading one shows old numbers after the base data changes. Test the refresh schedule and what the user sees in between.
Performance: a view isn't automatically fast. Views calling views calling views hide expensive joins, so EXPLAIN a query against the view (8.5).
## Triggers: code that fires by itself
A trigger is attached to a table and an event (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and runs BEFORE or AFTER it, once for each affected row (in MySQL). We created two. trg_leave_dates_bi rejects impossible dates before an insert, and trg_leave_status_audit writes a history row whenever status changes. Find the triggers:
```sql
SELECT trigger_name, action_timing, event_manipulation AS event, event_object_table AS on_table
FROM   information_schema.triggers WHERE trigger_schema = DATABASE();
-- PostgreSQL: pg_trigger / information_schema.triggers    SQL Server: sys.triggers
```

trigger_name           | action_timing | event  | on_table
trg_leave_dates_bi     | BEFORE        | INSERT | leave_requests
## trg_leave_status_audit | AFTER         | UPDATE | leave_requests

Testing a trigger means causing its event and checking the effect, in both the positive and negative directions:
-- A BEFORE trigger that rejects
```sql
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days)
VALUES (1, 1, '2026-12-10', '2026-12-05', 1);
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): end_date must not be before start_date
```

-- Statement atomicity: one bad row rejects the whole multi-row insert
```sql
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days) VALUES
(1, 1, '2026-12-01', '2026-12-01', 1),
(1, 1, '2026-12-10', '2026-12-05', 1);
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): end_date must not be before start_date   -- and the first row was NOT inserted (InnoDB)
```

-- An AFTER trigger that logs: fires once per changed row
```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE leave_requests SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE status = 'pending';
SELECT COUNT(*) AS history_rows_written FROM leave_status_history WHERE new_status = 'cancelled';   -- 3 (requests 1, 4, 9)
ROLLBACK;
```

## What to test around triggers:
Hidden side effects. The UI test for "cancel a request" now has a second assertion: the history row exists. If the application already wrote history itself, does it now appear twice (application plus trigger)? Query COUNT(*) per event.
Trigger versus app logic overlap. Duplicate or conflicting rules in both places are a top source of double-writes and inconsistent balances.
Bulk and import paths. An import that disables triggers (PostgreSQL session_replication_role = replica or ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER, SQL Server DISABLE TRIGGER; MySQL has no switch, so tools use a session variable checked inside the trigger) silently skips the audit trail and validation. After any load, run the consistency check from 6.3 (current state versus history).
Your own fixes fire triggers too. Setting a status back with an UPDATE to reset a test writes a history row (approved to pending), which will look like an illegal transition later (10.5). Clean those rows up as part of the reset.
Cascades and recursion. One update may fire a trigger that updates another table with its own trigger, and MySQL limits what a trigger can do to its own table. Confirm the total effect with a before/after snapshot (6.6).
Errors from triggers reach users. The SIGNAL message above is a developer-written string, so check what the UI shows when it fires (a friendly message, or the raw text).
Performance. A trigger that runs a heavy query executes once per row, so a bulk update of 50,000 rows runs it 50,000 times.
## Stored procedures: named code you call
A stored procedure bundles statements, variables, conditions and transactions on the server, and is called with CALL (MySQL and PostgreSQL 11+), EXEC (SQL Server). Some applications route most writes through procedures, with the API doing little beyond calling them. sp_approve_leave validates, deducts the balance and updates the status in one transaction. Its source is visible via SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE sp_approve_leave\G (MySQL), pg_get_functiondef() (PostgreSQL) or sp_helptext (SQL Server), and all routines are in information_schema.routines.
Test a procedure like any function: partition the inputs, hit the boundaries, and verify the outputs and the side effects.
```sql
CALL sp_approve_leave(999, 3);
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): Leave request not found
```

```sql
CALL sp_approve_leave(2, 3);
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): Only pending requests can be approved          (request 2 is already approved)
```

```sql
CALL sp_approve_leave(1, 2);
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): Employees cannot approve their own leave       (request 1 belongs to employee 2)
```

-- Atomicity: make the balance too low, then confirm that nothing moved
```sql
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 1.0 WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 1;
CALL sp_approve_leave(1, 1);
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): Insufficient leave balance
SELECT status FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id = 1;         -- still 'pending': the ROLLBACK worked
```

-- The happy path
```sql
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 18.0 WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 1;
CALL sp_approve_leave(1, 1);
```

Then verify every effect, including the one nobody mentioned:
```sql
SELECT lr.status, lr.approved_by, b.balance, b.version,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leave_status_history h
        WHERE h.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id AND h.old_status = 'pending' AND h.new_status = 'approved') AS approval_history_rows
FROM   leave_requests lr
JOIN   leave_balances b ON b.employee_id = lr.employee_id AND b.leave_type_id = lr.leave_type_id
WHERE  lr.leave_request_id = 1;
```

status   | approved_by | balance | version | approval_history_rows
## approved | 1           | 15.0    | 1       | 1

The procedure never inserts into leave_status_history. The trigger did that, an example of logic split across two objects, and a reminder to read all the objects attached to a table before deciding what an operation does. Calling the procedure a second time returns Only pending requests can be approved, so a retry doesn't deduct twice, which is the idempotency behaviour to look for (7.7).
More things to test in procedures: inputs at the edges (NULL arguments, negative IDs, an approver who doesn't exist, an inactive approver); permissions (which roles can EXECUTE it, 0.5, and whether a read-only account is really blocked); concurrency (two callers at once, 7.7, where the FOR UPDATE and the guarded UPDATE in this procedure are what should make one call fail cleanly); transaction handling (does an error path roll back, or leave partial work); and output shape (result sets and OUT parameters that the API depends on).
In automation, a procedure test looks like any other DB-level test:
```py
import pytest, pymysql
```

```py
def test_approve_leave_rejects_self_approval_and_changes_nothing(db):
    before = db_state(db, request_id=1)                       # helper: status, balance, history count
```

```sql
    with pytest.raises(pymysql.err.OperationalError) as exc:
        db.cursor().execute("CALL sp_approve_leave(%s, %s)", (1, 2))    # employee 2 approving their own request
    assert "cannot approve their own leave" in str(exc.value)
```

    assert db_state(db, request_id=1) == before               # atomicity: no partial change

| def test_approve_leave_success_changes_all_three_things(db): | db.cursor().execute("CALL sp_approve_leave(%s, %s)", (1, 1)) |
|---|---|
| s = db_state(db, request_id=1) | assert (s.status, s.balance, s.approved_history_rows) == ("approved", 15.0, 1) |

Dialect differences in one place

MySQL

| PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|
| Procedure call | CALL sp(...) |
| CALL sp(...) (procedures, 11+); functions via SELECT fn(...) | EXEC sp @a = 1, @b = 2 |
| Raise an error | SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = '...' |
| RAISE EXCEPTION '...' | THROW 50000, '...', 1 |
| Trigger scope | Per row only |
| Per row or per statement | Per statement (use inserted / deleted tables) |
| Disable a trigger | No switch |
| ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER | DISABLE TRIGGER ... ON ... |
| View definition | SHOW CREATE VIEW |
| pg_get_viewdef | sp_helptext |

SQL Server's per-statement triggers are a common source of bugs: a trigger written as if it saw one row misbehaves when a single UPDATE changes many rows.
## Where these go in later parts
Triggers and history tables come back in the approval workflow checks (10.5), and views feed dashboards and report validation (9.6). When you export or restore a database (11.2), remember that views, triggers and routines are separate objects that a "data only" export omits.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why learn the patterns
Application schemas are built from a handful of recurring designs. Once you recognise a pattern, you know its typical failure modes and can write the standard checks without studying the table from scratch. This chapter covers the four you'll meet in every module, then lists a few more.
## Soft deletes: rows that are "deleted" but still there
Instead of removing a row, the application sets a flag (is_deleted = 1) or a timestamp (deleted_at IS NOT NULL). Reasons: keep history and audit trails, allow undo, and avoid foreign key breakage. Costs: every query, screen, report, export, count and job must remember to exclude deleted rows, and forgetting is the most common data-visibility bug there is. Bikash (is_deleted = 1) is a soft-deleted employee: v_leave_summary hides him, a query without the filter would not.
## Standard soft-delete checks:
-- 1. Every place that should hide deleted rows: compare the raw count with the visible count
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, SUM(is_deleted = 0) AS visible, SUM(is_deleted = 1) AS hidden FROM employees;   -- 5 | 4 | 1
```

-- 2. Children of deleted parents (the logical orphans from 4.3)
```sql
SELECT lr.leave_request_id, lr.status, e.employee_id
FROM   leave_requests lr JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id
WHERE  e.is_deleted = 1 AND lr.status IN ('pending','approved');
```

-- 3. Inconsistent flags
```sql
SELECT employee_id, status, is_deleted FROM employees WHERE is_deleted = 1 AND status = 'active';    -- deleted but still "active"
```

Tester scenarios: delete through the UI, then confirm the row disappears from lists, search, dropdowns, dashboards, exports and API responses (but is still in the table); confirm login is blocked; check what happens to children (pending leave, appointments, payroll); try to restore; and check that COUNT tiles agree with what the lists show (2.1, 3.1).
## The soft-delete unique key trap
Look at employee_documents. Ravi's contract was soft-deleted, so uploading a new one should work:
```sql
INSERT INTO employee_documents (employee_id, doc_type, file_name, created_by)
VALUES (2, 'contract', 'ravi_contract_new.pdf', 1);
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '2-contract' for key 'employee_documents.uq_emp_doctype'
```

The "deleted" row still holds the unique key (employee_id, doc_type). Users see "you can't upload a contract" although they see none in the list, a bug that only appears after a delete and re-add. The obvious fix, adding deleted_at to the unique key, doesn't work in MySQL or PostgreSQL, because NULL never equals NULL: UNIQUE (employee_id, doc_type, deleted_at) would then allow two active rows (both with deleted_at = NULL). The correct fixes make the key apply only to active rows:
```sql
-- MySQL: a generated column that is 1 for active rows and NULL for deleted ones (NULLs don't collide)
ALTER TABLE employee_documents
  ADD COLUMN active_flag TINYINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (IF(deleted_at IS NULL, 1, NULL)) STORED,
  ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_emp_doctype_active (employee_id, doc_type, active_flag);
ALTER TABLE employee_documents DROP INDEX uq_emp_doctype;
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: a partial unique index
--   CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_emp_doctype_active ON employee_documents (employee_id, doc_type) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
-- SQL Server: a filtered unique index
--   CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_emp_doctype_active ON employee_documents (employee_id, doc_type) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

Now the re-upload succeeds, and a second active contract is still refused:
```sql
INSERT INTO employee_documents (employee_id, doc_type, file_name, created_by) VALUES (2, 'contract', 'ravi_contract_new.pdf', 1);   -- OK
INSERT INTO employee_documents (employee_id, doc_type, file_name, created_by) VALUES (2, 'contract', 'ravi_contract_v3.pdf', 1);
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '2-contract-1' for key 'employee_documents.uq_emp_doctype_active'
```

The test is a three-step scenario you can run on any soft-delete table with a unique rule: create, soft-delete, create again (must succeed), create a second active one (must fail). Also test the same flow for emails and usernames: can a deleted employee's email be reused for a new hire, and is that what the business wants?
## Audit columns: who and when
created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by (and sometimes deleted_by) record the row's history. Their value is only as good as their correctness, and they're checked by almost nobody, which is exactly why they're neglected. Checks:
```sql
SELECT 'updated_at earlier than created_at' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS violations
FROM   employee_documents WHERE updated_at < created_at
UNION ALL
SELECT 'created_by missing', COUNT(*) FROM employee_documents WHERE created_by IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'created_by points at a missing employee', COUNT(*)
FROM   employee_documents d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = d.created_by
WHERE  d.created_by IS NOT NULL AND e.employee_id IS NULL;
```

| check_name                              \| violations | updated_at earlier than created_at      \| 0 |
|---|---|
| created_by missing                      \| 1 | created_by points at a missing employee \| 0 |

Mina's certificate has no creator, which is the typical fingerprint of a code path that forgot to set it (an import, a background job, or an API endpoint that bypasses the usual user context). Scenario tests: create a record in the UI and check created_at and created_by (the logged-in user, not a service account); edit it and confirm updated_at moved and created_at and created_by did not; run an unrelated bulk operation and check updated_at is unchanged for rows it didn't touch; and confirm a no-change save either leaves updated_at alone or bumps it, according to the design. Remember the trap from 7.1: a column defined ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is bumped by any update, including a test-data fix, which may re-trigger sync jobs that watch for recent changes. And watch time zones: audit timestamps should be stored consistently (usually UTC) and displayed in the user's zone, and the offset between the database value and the screen is expected, not a bug (1.2).
## Status and enum columns: the state of a record
A status column drives workflows: what the user sees, which buttons appear, which reports include the row. Designs:

| Design | Example | Strength | Weakness | Native ENUM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| status ENUM('draft','processed','paid') | Compact, self-validating | Adding a value needs a DDL change (6.4); invalid-value behaviour depends on sql_mode | VARCHAR + CHECK | status VARCHAR(20) CHECK (status IN (...)) |
| Portable | Values repeated in code and DB, and can drift | Integer code | status_id TINYINT (1, 2, 3) | Compact |
| Unreadable in raw queries; the meaning lives in code or a lookup | Lookup table + FK | status_code referencing ref_payroll_status | One source of truth, extra columns (label, order, active) | Joins everywhere; the lookup can drift between environments (6.5) |

## Standard checks and scenarios:
-- Which statuses are actually in use, and how many rows each? (compare with the requirement's list)
```sql
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS rows_ FROM payroll GROUP BY status ORDER BY rows_ DESC;
```

| status    \| rows_ | processed \| 3 |
|---|---|
| paid      \| 3 | draft     \| 1 |

Then work through: each value renders correctly in the UI and in every language and export (a raw code like 2 or processed leaking onto a screen is a common defect); each value is reachable through the app (a state nothing ever produces, or that nothing can leave, is suspicious); an invalid value is rejected at API level ("status": "archived"), with strict mode off MySQL silently stores an empty string, so check SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payroll WHERE status = ''; every status is included or excluded correctly in counts and filters (the partition check, 2.1); and transitions obey the workflow. The database rarely stores which transitions are legal. That takes a history table and a rules table, and it's the whole subject of 10.5.
## Lookup (reference) tables: one place for shared values
Lookup tables hold small, slowly changing lists: departments, leave types, statuses, roles, countries, tax slabs. Other tables reference them by key. Our ref_payroll_status exists, but look at how it relates to the real column:
```sql
SELECT r.code AS lookup_code, r.is_active,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payroll p WHERE p.status = r.code) AS rows_using,
       LOCATE(CONCAT('''', r.code, ''''),
              (SELECT column_type FROM information_schema.columns
               WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'payroll' AND column_name = 'status')) > 0 AS in_payroll_enum
FROM   ref_payroll_status r ORDER BY r.sort_order;
```

lookup_code | is_active | rows_using | in_payroll_enum
| draft       \| 1         \| 1          \| 1 | processed   \| 1         \| 3          \| 1 |
|---|---|
| paid        \| 1         \| 3          \| 1 | cancelled   \| 0         \| 0          \| 0 |

The lookup lists cancelled (inactive) but payroll.status is a separate native enum that can't store it. Two sources of truth have drifted. The tester's questions: which one does the UI's dropdown read, and what happens when someone later activates cancelled in the lookup? Lookup-table checks in general:
Deactivating a value that's in use. Can an admin deactivate a leave type that still has pending requests or balances? What do existing rows show, and can new rows still pick it? (is_active = 0 should hide it from new-record dropdowns but still display it on old records.)
Renaming a value (the label vs the code). Historical reports should show what they showed before, or the new label consistently, according to the rule.
Ordering (sort_order) and duplicates (UNIQUE on the code and on the label).
Referential integrity: every code used in a business table exists in the lookup (the anti-join from 4.1). Hard-coded IDs in code (leave_type_id = 2 meaning Sick) break the moment IDs differ between environments (6.5).
Reference data drift between environments (6.5), such as Annual leave being 18 days in one and 20 in another, and the effect on every test that assumes a number.

| More patterns you'll meet | Pattern | What it looks like | Typical checks | Junction (many-to-many) table | employee_skills(employee_id, skill_id) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Duplicate pairs (composite unique), orphans on both sides, delete behaviour on either parent | Effective-dated rows | valid_from, valid_to on salary, tax rate, allowance rules | Overlaps (self join, 4.2), gaps (LAG, 5.5), exactly one open-ended current row | History/versioned table | A row per change (leave_status_history) |
| Current state equals last history row (6.3), legal transitions (10.5) | Multi-tenant column | company_id on every table | Every query and join filters it; test cross-tenant reads via the API | Money in minor units | Amount stored in paisa/cents as an integer |
| Conversion at the boundaries, rounding, display formatting | Sequence/number tables | Document or invoice numbers generated from a counter | Concurrency (7.7), gaps, format, resets each year | Polymorphic reference | entity_type + entity_id |
| No FK possible, so run orphan checks per type (6.3) | JSON column | Flexible settings or payload | Schema of the JSON, missing keys, querying with JSON_EXTRACT / ->> | Archive tables | Old rows moved to _archive |

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What testers can and can't do here
Performance tuning belongs to developers and DBAs, but you're often the first person to notice that "the report takes 40 seconds", and a report with evidence gets fixed while a vague complaint gets ignored. You need three skills: read an EXPLAIN plan well enough to spot the usual problems, measure a slowdown reliably, and recognise when to hand it over with the right evidence. (Full load and performance testing, 0.7, is out of scope.) Use att_big, the 20,000-row table, to practise.
## Why size and realism matter
On 10 rows, everything is fast, and the optimizer may even prefer a full scan because reading 10 rows is cheaper than using an index. Performance problems only appear with production-like data volume and distribution (7.5), on a server whose settings and indexes match production (6.5). A slow query on a tiny QA dataset is worth reporting, and a fast query there proves little.
```sql
EXPLAIN: ask the database how it will run the query
EXPLAIN in front of a SELECT (or UPDATE/DELETE) shows the plan without running the statement:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM att_big WHERE employee_id = 42;
```

id | select_type | table   | type | possible_keys | key  | key_len | ref  | rows  | filtered | Extra
1  | SIMPLE      | att_big | ALL  | NULL          | NULL | NULL    | NULL | 19870 | 10.00    | Using where

(Illustrative: rows is an estimate and differs between runs and servers.) The columns that matter:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Look for | type |
| How rows are accessed, best to worst: const/eq_ref (one row by key), ref (index lookup), range (index range), index (full index scan), ALL (full table scan) | ALL on a large table |
| possible_keys / key | Indexes that could be used / the one chosen |
| key = NULL on a big table | rows |
| Estimated rows the database must examine | Very large values next to a small result |
| filtered | Percent of examined rows expected to survive the WHERE |
| Low (10%) means 90% wasted work | Extra |
| Using filesort (sorted without an index), Using temporary (temp table), Using index (covered by the index, good), Using where | filesort or temporary on big sets |

Here the database has no index on employee_id, so it reads all 20,000 rows to find 40. Now add the index and compare:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_att_emp_date ON att_big (employee_id, work_date);
ANALYZE TABLE att_big;
```

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM att_big WHERE employee_id = 42;
```

id | select_type | table   | type | possible_keys    | key              | key_len | ref   | rows | filtered | Extra
1  | SIMPLE      | att_big | ref  | idx_att_emp_date | idx_att_emp_date | 4       | const | 40   | 100.00   | NULL

The plan shifted from ALL and about 19,900 examined rows to ref and 40. The leftmost-prefix rule (8.1) shows next:
```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM att_big WHERE work_date = '2025-01-10';
-- typically type: ALL again, because work_date isn't the leftmost column of idx_att_emp_date
```

Add a second index for that query, then compare a sargable filter with a function-wrapped one:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_att_date ON att_big (work_date);
```

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM att_big WHERE work_date >= '2025-01-01' AND work_date < '2025-01-11';   -- type: range, key: idx_att_date
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM att_big WHERE DATE_FORMAT(work_date, '%Y-%m') = '2025-01';              -- type: index or ALL: function on the column
```

The second query returns a related answer, but it cannot use the index to locate rows, so on a real table it scans everything (2.1). Sorting has its own signal:
```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM att_big ORDER BY hours DESC LIMIT 10;
-- Extra: Using filesort      (no index on hours: sorts all rows, then keeps 10)
```

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE and measured plans
EXPLAIN shows estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+, PostgreSQL, SQL Server via "actual execution plan") runs the query and shows real timings and row counts:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM att_big WHERE employee_id = 42\G
-- -> Index lookup on att_big using idx_att_emp_date (employee_id=42)  (cost=14 rows=40) (actual time=0.05..0.12 rows=40 loops=1)
```

Compare estimated with actual rows. A large gap means stale statistics (ANALYZE TABLE in MySQL, ANALYZE in PostgreSQL) or skewed data. PostgreSQL's version looks like this, and again shows a scan-versus-index difference:
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM att_big WHERE employee_id = 42;
 Seq Scan on att_big  (cost=0.00..389.00 rows=40 width=32) (actual time=0.02..2.10 rows=40 loops=1)
   Filter: (employee_id = 42)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 19960
 Execution Time: 2.2 ms
```

Rows Removed by Filter: 19960 is the plain-English form of "it read everything to keep 40". Warning: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. On an UPDATE or DELETE it really changes data, so wrap it in a transaction and roll back (7.3), and never use it casually on a shared or production-like server.

| Signs of trouble, and the usual cause | Symptom in the plan or behaviour | Usual cause | What to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| type = ALL on a big table | Missing index, or index not usable | SHOW INDEX, sargability (2.1) | Index exists but key = NULL |
| Function on the column, leading wildcard, type mismatch, low selectivity | Rewrite the filter; compare column and value types | Using filesort / Using temporary on large sets | Sort or group has no supporting index |
| Index on the sort/group columns | Huge rows in a join | Join column not indexed (no FK index in PostgreSQL/SQL Server) | Indexes on the child's FK column |
| Fast for one user, slow for a list of 100 | N+1 queries: one query per row (5.1) | Count queries per request in the API or query log | Slow only at page 500 |
| Deep OFFSET: skips 10,000 rows first (2.2) | Keyset pagination | Slow only in one environment | Different volume, missing index, stale statistics, different version/settings (6.5) |
| Compare plans across environments | Fast the second run, slow the first | Cold cache | Repeat runs, and note both |

## Measure honestly
A single timing tells you little. Run the query 3 to 5 times and record the first (cold) and the median. Use the same data and parameters each time. Separate the layers: database time (EXPLAIN ANALYZE or the client's execution time), API time, and full page time. Include the row counts and environment, and record the parameters, because the same query is instant for one employee and slow for the largest department. In automation, a simple timing budget on the API turns "feels slow" into a repeatable check:
```ts
test('attendance API stays under 500 ms at 20k rows', async ({ request }) => {
| const times: number[] = []; | for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { | const t0 = Date.now(); | const res = await request.get('/api/attendance?employeeId=42'); | expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy(); | times.push(Date.now() - t0); |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| } | times.sort((a, b) => a - b); | const median = times[2]; | console.log('timings ms', times); | expect(median, `median of ${times}`).toBeLessThan(500);          // budget agreed with the team, not invented | }); |
```

The budget must come from a requirement or team agreement. A number you pick to make the test pass is worthless. And network jitter on shared infrastructure makes small budgets flaky, so use medians and generous margins.
## Finding slow queries
The usual sources, in the order a tester meets them: the slow query log (MySQL slow_query_log, long_query_time; PostgreSQL log_min_duration_statement), usually enabled by DBAs; pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL) and MySQL's performance_schema / sys schema (sys.statement_analysis), which rank statements by total time and can be read-only for you; APM tools (Datadog, New Relic, Grafana) that show queries per request; the browser's network tab, which tells you which API call is slow; and the application's own debug or SQL logging in test environments. "Which query does this screen run?" is answered fastest by asking a developer to turn on SQL logging for a QA build, and then you can EXPLAIN those statements yourself.
## Concurrency and locks also look like slowness
If a query is fast in your client but the screen hangs, the cause may be waiting, not work: a long-running transaction holding locks (7.3, 7.7), a report locking a table, or a migration in progress (6.4). Check for blocking sessions before blaming the query (SHOW PROCESSLIST, information_schema.innodb_trx, PostgreSQL pg_stat_activity and pg_locks).
## What NOT to do
Don't create indexes on a shared database "to see if it helps" (they slow writes for everyone and may not be allowed, 0.5). Don't run heavy EXPLAIN ANALYZE or full-table COUNT(*) on a production-like server during working hours. Don't tune a query in isolation and claim victory (a faster query on your data might be slower on production's distribution). Don't SELECT * from huge tables to "just look" (use LIMIT, and EXPLAIN first).
## When to escalate, and with what
Escalate when the plan shows a full scan on a large table, when the slowdown grows with data volume, when the evidence points to a missing index or a structural problem, or when the fix would need DDL you can't run. A good escalation includes:
The user-visible symptom and the requirement or budget it breaks ("Payroll report loads in 38 s, target 5 s").
The exact query (from the log or a developer), and the parameters that reproduce it.
Data volumes: row counts of the tables involved, and how they compare with production.
The plan: EXPLAIN (and EXPLAIN ANALYZE if safe), with the worrying lines highlighted (type: ALL, rows: 19870, Using filesort).
Timings: cold and median, in which environment, at what time.
What you already ruled out (locks, environment differences, cache).
A hypothesis, stated as a hypothesis ("an index on (employee_id, work_date) is missing in QA and present in staging (see drift check)").
That is a ticket a developer can act on in minutes. Chapters 6.5 and 11.3 cover the drift comparison and packaging the output.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## A method, so you're not just clicking around
On a new project you'll often be handed a connection string and told "the data is in there". A structured exploration takes an afternoon instead of weeks, and it produces a document the whole team can use. The steps below go from broad to specific, and every one is read-only, so it's safe on shared environments. Practise them on hrms_practice as if you'd never seen it.
## Step 0: get oriented and stay safe
Confirm the environment and your access (0.4, 0.5). Ask for a read-only account, ideally on a replica (11.2), and check what you're connected to:
```sql
SELECT DATABASE() AS db, @@hostname AS host, @@version AS version, USER() AS you, CURRENT_USER() AS effective_user;
```

Also note the server settings that change behaviour (6.5): sql_mode, collation, time zone. Keep queries cheap, with LIMIT and EXPLAIN first on anything unfamiliar, and avoid SELECT * on tables of unknown size.
Step 1: inventory the tables
```sql
SELECT table_name, table_type, table_rows AS est_rows,
       ROUND((data_length + index_length) / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS size_mb, create_time, update_time
FROM   information_schema.tables
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE()
ORDER  BY table_type, (data_length + index_length) DESC;
```

table_name            | table_type | est_rows | size_mb | create_time         | update_time
att_big               | BASE TABLE | 19870    | 1.52    | 2026-09-21 09:10:44 | 2026-09-21 09:11:02
attendance            | BASE TABLE | 8        | 0.05    | 2026-09-21 08:00:12 | 2026-09-21 08:30:20
employees             | BASE TABLE | 5        | 0.06    | ...                 | ...
leave_requests        | BASE TABLE | 9        | 0.08    | ...                 | ...
...
## v_leave_summary       | VIEW       | NULL     | NULL    | NULL                | NULL

(Illustrative.) Read it for orientation: which tables are big (where performance matters, 8.5), which are tiny (likely lookups), which change often (update_time, useful for finding the tables a screen writes), and which are views. table_rows is an estimate for InnoDB and can be far off, so use COUNT(*) for exact numbers and never as an assertion (3.1). Also list the non-table objects:
```sql
SELECT routine_type, routine_name FROM information_schema.routines  WHERE routine_schema = DATABASE();
SELECT trigger_name, event_object_table FROM information_schema.triggers WHERE trigger_schema = DATABASE();
```

## Step 2: learn the naming conventions and find things
Look for patterns: snake_case or tblCamelCase, plural or singular, prefixes (tbl_, ref_, mst_ for master data, trn_ for transactions, _hist, _archive), suffixes (_id, _code, _flag, _dt), and legacy abbreviations (emp, dept, lv). Then search by keyword across the whole schema:
-- Where does the word "leave" appear in a table name or column name?
```sql
SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND (table_name LIKE '%leave%' OR column_name LIKE '%leave%')
ORDER  BY table_name, ordinal_position;
```

-- Every status-like column and what it can hold
```sql
SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND (column_name LIKE '%status%' OR column_name LIKE '%state%' OR data_type = 'enum');
```

## Step 3: read the structure of the important tables
For each table that matters, read the complete DDL (SHOW CREATE TABLE, 7.4), then apply the 8.2 checklist: types, nullability, defaults, enums, keys, constraints, soft-delete and audit columns.
## Step 4: map the relationships
List the foreign keys (the query in 4.3) to draw the graph: which tables are parents, which are children, which are the hubs (employees is referenced by nearly everything). Where a _id column has no FK, note it as a suspected relationship and confirm with an orphan query or a developer. To see it as a picture, generate an ER diagram: DBeaver (right-click the database, then View Diagram), MySQL Workbench (Reverse Engineer), pgAdmin's ERD tool, or SchemaSpy for a browsable HTML report. Appendix E holds the ER overview for our sample database.
## Step 5: profile the data
Structure tells you what can be stored, and profiling tells you what is. For a table, look at row counts, value ranges, null counts, distinct counts and the most common values:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                          AS total_rows,
       COUNT(manager_id)                 AS manager_id_filled,
       COUNT(DISTINCT department_id)     AS distinct_departments,
       MIN(hire_date)                    AS earliest_hire,   MAX(hire_date) AS latest_hire,
       SUM(is_deleted = 1)               AS soft_deleted
FROM   employees;
```

```sql
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees GROUP BY status ORDER BY n DESC;         -- low-cardinality columns: see the actual values
SELECT * FROM leave_requests ORDER BY leave_request_id DESC LIMIT 10;                 -- a look at recent rows, on tables that are safe to sample
```

The profile answers practical questions. Is a column always filled, or mostly NULL? Are there suspicious values (dates in 1970 or 2099, negative amounts, an empty-string status)? Are the sample values production-like or obviously artificial? To profile every column of a table without typing each query, let SQL write them:
```sql
SELECT CONCAT('SELECT ''', column_name, ''' AS col, COUNT(*) AS total, COUNT(`', column_name, '`) AS non_null, ',
              'COUNT(DISTINCT `', column_name, '`) AS distinct_vals FROM `', table_name, '`;') AS profiling_sql
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'employees'
ORDER  BY ordinal_position;
```

Run the generated statements (or wrap them in UNION ALL). Be careful with personal data: sampling production-like tables shows real values, so keep them out of screenshots and bug reports (7.6).
## Step 6: connect the UI to the tables
This is where the exploration pays off. For each important screen, find which tables it reads and writes:
Probe with a unique value. Create a record in the UI with a recognisable string (QA_Probe_7731 as a name or note), then search every text column for it. SQL can generate the searches:
```sql
SELECT CONCAT('SELECT ''', table_name, '.', column_name, ''' AS hit, COUNT(*) AS n FROM `', table_name,
              '` WHERE `', column_name, '` LIKE ''%QA_Probe_7731%'';') AS stmt
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND data_type IN ('varchar','char','text','mediumtext','longtext');
```

Running the output and keeping the rows with n > 0 shows every table and column the app wrote your string to, including audit and log tables you didn't know about. For numbers or dates you can't search this way, use the before/after snapshot (6.6) or look at rows changed since a timestamp (created_at or updated_at greater than the moment of your action, on the tables with recent update_time).
Watch the traffic. The browser's network tab shows the API call, and a developer can show you the SQL it runs.
Follow one record. Pick a single employee and trace them through every table (WHERE employee_id = 2 in each child table). Their trail through leave_requests, attendance, payroll, leave_balances and leave_status_history teaches you the module more quickly than any diagram.
## Step 7: read the logic that lives in the database
List and read the views, triggers, routines and check constraints (8.3, 8.1). This is where hidden rules live, such as the is_deleted = 0 inside v_leave_summary and the history rows the trigger writes.
## Step 8: identify reference data and its meaning
Small tables (a handful of rows) are usually lookups: read them all, and note what each code means, since raw values like status_code = 'R' are meaningless without them (6.1). Look for magic numbers and codes used in code and queries, and ask what they stand for.
Step 9: write it down
Keep a living document, in the format your team can maintain:

| Table | Purpose | Key columns | Written by (screen/API) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read by (screens/reports) | Notes / rules | leave_requests | One row per leave application |
| leave_request_id; status, approved_by | Apply Leave, Approvals | Leave list, dashboard, v_leave_summary | Trigger writes history on status change; days is working days |
| leave_balances | Remaining days per employee and type | PK (employee_id, leave_type_id); version | Approval procedure |
| Balance widget | Optimistic-lock version | payroll | Monthly pay |
| (employee_id, pay_month) | Payroll run | Payslips, reports | No unique constraint; net = basic + allowances - deductions |

Add a short glossary of terms and codes (this feeds Appendix C) and a list of open questions (8.2). Save your best exploratory queries with comments, because they become the reusable sanity checks in Part 10.
## Step 10: ask the people who know
Bring specific questions to developers, analysts and DBAs: "Which tables does the Apply Leave screen write?", "Is approved_by ever NULL for approved requests?", "Are there scheduled jobs that update this table?", "Which tables can I ignore?", "Which are the archive and reporting copies?", "What changed recently?" An hour with the developer who built the module, with your notes in hand, is worth days of solo guessing, and it makes the questions in your document precise.
## Common traps while exploring
Confusing similar names (employee vs employees vs employee_master), or two schemas with copies of the same table (stale reporting tables).
Trusting table_rows or an empty table as "unused" (it may only be filled by a scheduled job).
Reading only production-like data from one environment. QA's values may be artificial, so compare across environments (6.5).
Missing the soft-delete flag or the tenant column and concluding the counts don't match the UI (8.4).
Assuming a column's meaning from its name (status, type, flag, amount). Check the values and ask.
Exposing personal data in notes, screenshots or chat (7.6).
## Where this leads
The map you build here is the starting point for the test design in 8.2, the sanity queries in 10.2, the API-to-database checks in Part 9, and the reference sections in Appendices C and E.

## Cleanup: put the sample database back
Run this to undo Part 8's demo changes. The trigger, procedure, view, CHECK constraint, ref_payroll_status and employee_documents stay, because later Parts reuse them. The UPDATE fires the audit trigger, so the history rows it writes are removed afterwards.
```sql
UPDATE leave_requests SET status = 'pending', approved_by = NULL WHERE leave_request_id = 1;
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 18.0, version = 0 WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 1;
DELETE FROM leave_status_history
WHERE  leave_request_id = 1 AND NOT (old_status IS NULL AND new_status = 'pending');   -- keep only the original "created" row
```

```sql
DROP TABLE att_big, ux_demo;
```

If you also want a clean slate for the soft-delete demo, run DELETE FROM employee_documents WHERE file_name = 'ravi_contract_new.pdf';.
